newsitem.title: PERU: Peru '96 economic growth seen under 3 pct target.
newsitem.headline: Peru '96 economic growth seen under 3 pct target.

text.p: Weaker-than-expected September economic growth figures leave Peru likely to register an annual figure below the government's bottom target of three percent, according to local analysts consulted by Reuters.

They said growth could pick up slightly in the final quarter, but not sufficiently to take the overall gross domestic product (GDP) above the government's estimate of between 3.0 percent and 4.5 percent agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

According to the National Institute of Statistics and Information (INEI) figures released late Wednesday, the economy grew 1.9 percent in the first nine months of the year, compared to 8.9 percent in the same period of 1995.
Year-on-year GDP growth was 0.4 percent in September, compared with 3.9 percent year-on-year growth in the same month last year.

The figures were "very bad," said Pablo Secada, macroeconomic analyst at Santander Investment in Lima, who had been expecting a monthly figure of 3.5 percent and a January- September growth of between 2.1 percent and 2.2 percent.
"We have stopped seeing the recovery we saw between May and July, and I think October will be bad as well," he said.
Santander is currently revising its previous estimate of 3.5 percent growth in 1996.
"It is likely to be below three percent," said Secada, adding that there would be a minor recovery in November and December.

Among factors behind September's figures, he highlighted a strike that affected output at Peru's only iron producer Shougang, that was only partly compensated by increased production from other parts of the mining sector.

He also pointed to weaker growth in a category for the government's GDP figures called "others" -- including the banking, insurance, transport and government sectors -- that accounts for 30 percent of the overall figure.
Elmer Cuba, an analyst at Lima-based consultancy Macroconsult, said September's "bad news" would increase uncertainty in Peru's financial markets.
"It will have a negative impact since companies will hold their short-term investment decisions," she said. "They are going to wait to see what happens in coming months."

"The market was betting on a recovery. Everyone expected third quarter (year-on-year) growth of between 3.0 and 3.5 percent," she said. The actual third quarter figure was 2.4 percent, according to the INEI.
"I don't believe the government will be able to meet its target of between 3.0 percent and 4.5 percent for the year," she added. "I think we will finish the year at 2.8 percent."
Oscar Jasaui, head of the Lima chamber of economists, was less pessimistic than the majority of analysts, saying the government was still on target for three percent growth this year.
"From where we are now, it is easy to reach three percent," he said.

He added that September's figures were adversely affected by the depreciation in that month of the local sol currency, but he said the figure may also appear unrealistically weak due to the exceptional comparative growth figure for the same month of 1995.
In 1995, Peru's economy expanded 7.0 percent, Latin America's second-highest growth rate, down from 13.1 percent in 1994, according to revised Central Reserve Bank figures.
